title: Keeping it abroad (Daniel 1)
hook: young exiles keep their food laws at the king's court

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther went in to the king uncalled, and named Haman, the enemy, at her own table. Your line was if I perish, I perish. Who did you speak up for? Today, a new book, and another royal court. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

A plate arrives from the king's own table. In Babylon, King Nebuchadnezzar has ordered some of the young captives from Judah to be trained for his court: good-looking, quick, skilled in learning. They'll be taught the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans. They'll eat the king's food and drink the king's wine. Among them are four young men: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. And the first thing the court does is rename them. Daniel becomes Belteshazzar. Hananiah becomes Shadrach, Mishael becomes Meshach, Azariah becomes Abed-nego. New names, a new language, new books. They accept all of it. Then the plate comes, and Daniel draws a line.
screen: `CAPTIVES TRAINED FOR THE KING.` → `FOUR NEW NAMES.` → `THEN THE KING'S PLATE.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank." Purposed in his heart. The decision is made inside before it's said out loud. The text doesn't spell out why the king's food would defile him. Some readers point to the food laws of the Torah. Some say the food and wine had been offered to idols. Some hear something simpler: a captive who won't depend on the king's table for everything. What the text does show is how he does it. He doesn't make a scene. He asks the official in charge, who is afraid: if these young men look worse than the others, the king will have his head. So Daniel offers a test. "Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink." Pulse means plain food from seeds: vegetables, beans. Ten days later, the text says, they look healthier than all the young men who ate the king's portion. And God, it adds, gave the four of them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom. So they study Babylon's books, answer to Babylon's names, serve Babylon's king, and still keep one thing that marks who they are. That's the shape of this story: live fully where you are, and keep something the place can't take away.
screen: `NEW NAMES, NEW LANGUAGE, NEW FOOD.` · then, large: `DANIEL PURPOSED IN HIS HEART.` · `A POLITE TEN-DAY TEST.` · `PULSE AND WATER.` · then: `LIVE THERE. KEEP ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to keep one practice in a strange place. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Choose one small thing you do that marks who you are. A blessing before you eat. A minute of quiet. A candle. A word of thanks before sleep. Now find the place where it's hardest to keep: a work trip, a friend's house, a loud lunchroom, a hospital, a day when you're simply tired. See yourself there. See yourself doing your small thing anyway, quietly, without a speech. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for help keeping it. The bell holds the time.
Pulse. The plain food of vegetables and beans Daniel asked for instead of the king's meat and wine. Today's word.
Your line: keep it abroad. Today, do your small thing in the place where it's least convenient, and do it politely. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher find ways to keep it while traveling, at work and at other people's tables, and the story of Daniel and his friends is told as an example of keeping Jewish practice far from home.

fork.setup: you're Daniel, a young captive at the king's court. you've taken a new name and new lessons. now the king's own food arrives. what do you do?
options: eat it; you've already given up so much.
refuse loudly in front of the court.
ask quietly for a ten-day test of pulse and water.
fork.reveal: he asks politely for a test, "prove thy servants... ten days", and at the end of it the four look healthier than the rest.

original.note: Hebrew: and Daniel set it upon his heart, the start of Daniel 1:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old story about eating your vegetables.
what it means: young captives accept new names and new learning, but keep one line: they won't defile themselves with the king's food.
what a scholar hears: the text never says exactly why. readers point to the food laws, to food offered to idols, or to not depending on the king's table.
